headline: Amazon Deforestation Hits Record Low, Falling 42% in a Year

summary_short: Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has plummeted to its lowest level ever recorded, with forest clearing falling 42% to an area smaller than the Spanish island of Mal…
body:
Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has plummeted to its lowest level on record, offering a rare moment of environmental progress in a region facing mounting pressures. New data from Brazil's national space research institute, INPE, reveals that forest clearing over the 12 months ended July 31, 2026, amounted to just 3,335 square kilometers—roughly the size of the Spanish island of Mallorca and representing a 42% drop from the previous year. The decline extends beyond the rainforest itself: the Cerrado, a wooded savanna adjacent to the Amazon, saw deforestation fall 24% to 5,516 square kilometers, also marking its lowest recorded level. These figures matter because they suggest that targeted conservation efforts can work, even in one of the world's most threatened ecosystems.

The turnaround accelerated sharply after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva took office in 2023, restoring environmental law enforcement, expanding conservation programs, and formally recognizing Indigenous territories—moves that have proven effective in slowing forest loss. Yet this progress faces serious headwinds. A re-election bid scheduled for later this month could reshape Brazil's Amazon policy, with seven of the nine Amazon state governors allied with a frontrunner who has campaigned on reducing protections for the forest. Beyond politics, climate conditions present another obstacle: scientists are warning of a super El Niño brewing in the Pacific, which typically triggers drought and increased fire risk in the southern Amazon.

The stakes are existential. The Amazon now contains about 15% deforestation; scientists warn that reaching 20-25% could cause the region's evapotranspiration system—the mechanism that drives rainfall across South America—to collapse. Such disruption could reduce rainfall in the continent's agricultural heartland, rippling far beyond Brazil's borders. For now, this year's data offers hope that the forest's decline is not inevitable.
quick_facts: 3,335 sq km cleared in 12 months—smaller than Mallorca island
42% drop in Amazon deforestation compared to previous year
Cerrado savanna also hit record low at 5,516 sq km
Brazil accounts for just over 60% of the Amazon rainforest
Risk of ecological collapse if deforestation reaches 20-25%
